newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Strike impact on SAfrican ports limited -officials.
newsitem.headline: Strike impact on SAfrican ports limited -officials.

text.p: A 24-hour-long strike called by South Africa's largest trade union federation to protest against new labour legislation had not caused major disruptions to the country's harbours, officials said on Monday.

Durban, the busiest harbour in Africa, had originally reported a 50 percent stayaway, but this later dropped to 16 percent as workers came to work late because of strike-affected transport, said Portnet spokeswoman Yvonne de Kock.
"The worst affected sections were cartage and the container terminals where only 20 to 30 percent of the workforce came to work," de Kock told Reuters.
Other sections had reported between 80 and 100 percent attendence, she added. "There has been no major disruption to the harbour."
There were about eight ships lying at anchor outside the harbour, but a regular flow of ships into and out of the port could be observed during the course of the day.
Port Elizabeth harbour authorities said about 35 percent of its 1,000-strong workforce had stayed off work, but alternate working arrangements had been made to minimise disruptions.
"We haven't had any major upheavals and our working rate has been largely unaffected," spokeswoman Hanlie Botha told Reuters.
The Richards Bay Coal Terminal had a stayaway of 20 percent, but a spokesman said it had not affected operations because extra workers were brought in to supplement the staff who had come to work.
The terminal loads an average of 180,000 tonnes of coal onto ships per day.
Richards Bay harbour authorities said there was a noticeable absenteeism, but did not have figures on how many people had come to work or which sections were worst affected.
Cape Town port officials could not be reached for comment but said earlier on Monday that disruptions were minimal and shipping had not been affected.
The 1.9 million strong Congress of South African Trade Unions called the strike to back its calls for a 40-hour working week, six months maternity leave and double pay for Sunday work.
